Reward encoding in mPFC GCaMP signals — pooled across both cohorts

All 11 mice from FP1 (younger) and FP2 (older) combined into one dataset, to test whether the RPE-related encoding found separately in each cohort holds up — and how much power pooling adds — before any age comparison is attempted.

Summary

Yes — the encoding is consistent across all 11 animals

This report combines the two independently-analyzed cohorts (7 younger FP1 mice, 4 older FP2 mice) into a single 11-animal, 64-session pool, and reruns the same pooled GLMs and within-animal RPE analyses on the union. The question motivating this step was simple: is the reward/value encoding found in each cohort separately a shared property of the same underlying signal, or two cohort-specific effects that happen to look similar? The answer, on every measure that can be checked at the animal level, is consistency — not two effects, one effect seen twice.

Headline result. Pooling adds the statistical power neither cohort had alone: the within-animal RPE-regression Wilcoxon test, non-significant in FP2 alone (p=0.125, the best possible at n=4) and only marginal in FP1 alone (p=0.016, n=7), is now solidly significant at n=11 (p=0.001), with 11/11 mice individually negative. The temporal-specificity control replicates exactly: 11/11 mice show a significant outcome×value interaction after the event, 0/11 before it — the same clean dissociation found in each cohort separately, now confirmed in every single animal across both.

How the cohorts compare

Two independent replications, then the pooled estimate

Nothing was refit from raw data for this step — the per-session PETH windows, trial tables, and FIR design matrices already extracted for the FP1 and FP2 reports were concatenated directly (mouse IDs don't overlap, both cohorts share an identical PETH time grid and FIR design, verified before merging) and the same analysis scripts rerun on the union.

The pooled R² values land between the two cohorts, as expected for a trial-count-weighted average (FP1 contributes more trials, so the pooled estimate sits closer to FP1's). This is a sanity check, not a new finding: if FP2 had been a fluke or an artifact of a smaller, different cohort, the pooled numbers would look like an average pulled toward wherever the larger sample sits with a wider spread — instead every per-mouse effect below points the same direction in both cohorts.

Model 1 — Time-resolved encoding GLM

The same regression, refit on the full pool

Identical specification to both cohort reports, refit on all 26,296 trials from all 11 mice together.

Z ~ Choice * Reward + Reward_lag1 + Reward_lag2 + Reward_lag3 + Q_diff_abs + C(Behavioral_State)

Same shape as both individual-cohort figures: Reward steps sharply at t=0 and holds; model fit is low and flat pre-event, rising sharply after; the three reward-history lags ramp smoothly with no discontinuity at the event. Pooling more than 1.5× the trials of either cohort alone sharpens the confidence bands without changing the qualitative picture.

Within-animal analyses

The pre-specified confirmatory tests, now across all 11 mice

The same four pre-specified analyses from both cohort reports, refit within each of the 11 mice individually and compared with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test across the full set — the test neither cohort had enough animals to power on its own.

1. Within-animal RPE regression

Post-event amplitude (mean z-score, 0–1 s after side-port entry) regressed on RPE_signed alone, separately per mouse.

All 11/11 mice show a significant negative βRPE (range −0.56 to −2.38, individually p from 1.8×10−2 to 1.6×10−138). With the full 11-animal set, the group-level Wilcoxon test that couldn't reach significance in either cohort alone is now clearly significant: p=0.001 (median βRPE = −0.861). As in both individual reports, letting outcome and value load freely (outcome × Q(chosen) interaction) shows a negative, significant interaction in 11/11 mice (p from 1.8×10−2 to 1.8×10−18).

2. Temporal specificity: does the value modulation appear before the event too?

The interaction above refit with pre_amp (−1 to 0 s before side-port entry) as the outcome, per mouse.

Vanishes cleanly in every animal. Post-event: significant in 11/11 mice, uniformly negative. Pre-event: significant in 0/11 mice (all p > 0.08), sign inconsistent across animals. This is the strongest version of the temporal control across the whole dataset: not one of the 11 mice shows a pre-existing value signal before the outcome that could explain the post-event effect away.

3. Signed vs. unsigned RPE

5-fold cross-validated out-of-sample R², per mouse, comparing signed vs. unsigned RPE as a predictor.

Still not confirmatory, but closer. 7/11 mice show signed beating unsigned; Wilcoxon p=0.067 — a trend, not significance at the conventional threshold, but noticeably closer than either cohort alone (FP1: p=0.22; FP2: p=0.25). This is the one test where pooling moved the result meaningfully rather than just tightening it — consistent with a real but smaller effect that neither 7 nor 4 animals alone could reliably detect, though it still isn't established at n=11.

4. Between-animal variability of the two pooled models

Both GLMs refit separately per mouse — encoding-model peak R² and FIR out-of-sample R², one point per animal, all 11 together.

Two things stand out once all 11 mice sit on the same axis. First, WCL25 and WCL26 (both FP1) are the clear low-water mark on both models — lowest encoding peak R² (0.156 and 0.176) and by far the lowest FIR R² (0.079 and 0.048, well below every other mouse's 0.14–0.46 range) — and they are also the two mice with the fewest trials (885 and 735, against 1,800–3,600 for the rest) and fewest sessions in the original cohort. This is exactly the pattern that prompted the hypothesis that these two animals may not have fully learned the task yet in the sessions available; nothing here proves that, but it is consistent with it, and distinguishes a plausible behavioral/developmental explanation from generic noise, since both metrics agree and both animals are the trial-count outliers too.

Second, WCL31 is unremarkable here. Within FP2's own 4-mouse comparison it looked like the weakest link across several unrelated tests; against the full 11-mouse pool its FIR R² (0.199) and encoding peak R² (0.218) sit squarely in the middle of the distribution, not near either tail. That earlier flag was almost certainly an artifact of comparing it against only 3 other animals rather than a real property of that mouse — a useful caution about reading too much into rank-order comparisons within a small cohort.

Interpretation

One effect, seen in both cohorts, now confirmed at full strength

Pooling both cohorts answers the question it was run to answer: the reward-locked signal and its value-dependent, outcome-specific modulation are not cohort-specific artifacts of FP1 or FP2 individually — they are properties of the same effect, present in all 11 mice regardless of which cohort they came from. The clearest evidence of this is the temporal-specificity result (Analysis 2 in each cohort report, Analysis 4's numbering here): 11 for 11 mice show the effect after the event and 0 for 11 show it before, with no exceptions in either cohort. The RPE regression, borderline in FP1 and underpowered in FP2, becomes unambiguous once pooled — not because pooling manufactures significance, but because 11/11 mice individually already showed the effect and the group test only needed enough animals to say so formally.

The one test that moved the most with pooling — signed vs. unsigned RPE, from non-significant in both cohorts to a trend at n=11 — is the most likely candidate for a real, smaller effect that would firm up further as the "at least another 12 mice" planned for this cohort are added. The two weakest-fitting animals (WCL25, WCL26) remain a genuine open question rather than noise: both metrics and their low trial counts agree, which is the pattern expected if they simply hadn't learned the task as well in the sessions captured, and is worth checking directly against their raw behavioral learning curves before the age comparison.

Ready for the next step. With RPE encoding now confirmed consistent across the full dataset, the planned next analysis — comparing FP1 (younger) against FP2 (older) directly, e.g. per-mouse βRPE or peak R² as a function of age/cohort — rests on solid ground: any age effect found there would be a difference layered on top of a shared encoding mechanism, not a confound from comparing two unrelated signals.

Scope. This covers only the “none” condition in both cohorts. The pooled R² values are trial-count-weighted averages, not a claim that the effect is uniform in size across cohorts (Model 1's peak R² genuinely differs, 0.20 vs. 0.30) — only that its direction and outcome-locked timing are uniform. WCL25/WCL26's low fit quality is flagged as a hypothesis (incomplete learning), not resolved here.
